extracted.intended_audience: researchers of peer review and scholarly publishing, conference organizers, and policy-makers interested in review format effects
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation of how switching from single-blind to double-blind peer review affects reviewer behavior, bias (especially prestige bias), and selection quality at a major computer science conference (ICLR). Uses analysis of peer-review files across the policy change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction in prestige bias (reviewer scores)
rubrics_metrics.description: After switching to double-blind review, the scores given to the most prestigious authors significantly decreased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether reviewer scores for papers by high-prestige authors drop under double-blind relative to single-blind. Measure statistical significance of score changes and consider subgroup analyses by author prestige. Note that a decrease in scores is evidence of reduced prestige-related favoritism but must be interpreted relative to acceptance thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on acceptance decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many of these papers were above the threshold for acceptance, the change did not affect paper acceptance decisions significantly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate not only score shifts but whether those shifts change final accept/reject outcomes. Consider acceptance thresholds and how many affected papers sit near the decision boundary — score changes that do not cross the threshold may not alter acceptance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection quality as measured by post-rejection citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers rejected in the single-blind format are cited more than those rejected under the double-blind format, suggesting that double-blind review better identifies poorer quality papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use downstream citation counts (or other impact proxies) of rejected papers to infer whether selection quality improved. Compare citation distributions of rejected papers across formats; treat citation counts as imperfect proxies for quality and control for time-since-publication and field effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating-scale effects and confounding measurement changes
rubrics_metrics.description: An apparently unrelated change — the change of rating scale from 10 to 4 points — likely reduced prestige bias significantly, to an extent that affected papers' acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating review-format interventions, control for simultaneous procedural or measurement changes (e.g., rating scale alterations) that can themselves affect bias or outcomes. Analyze how scale granularity influences reviewer discrimination and bias, and disentangle scale effects from anonymity effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on other (non-author-prestige) biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-blind peer review may have improved the quality of the selections by limiting other (non-author-prestige) biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate multiple bias types (e.g., institutional prestige, geographic, gender, topical) beyond author prestige. Look for differential changes across groups and examine whether anonymity reduces a range of identifiable biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical design: analysis of peer-review files before and after policy change
rubrics_metrics.description: The study analyzes the peer review files of 5,027 papers submitted to ICLR, which changed its reviewing policy from single-blind to double-blind in 2018.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use large-scale, before-and-after (quasi-experimental) data from a single venue to estimate policy impacts. Report sample sizes, time windows, and data provenance; address threats to causal inference such as concurrent policy/organizational changes and time trends.
